title: Utah's 3rd Congressional District Election, 2026
description: This race is for Utah's newly redrawn 3rd Congressional District, created after court-ordered redistricting shifted the state's congressional map. The district stretches from northern Utah to the Arizona border, encompassing Provo, Park City, and all five of Utah's national parks. The Republican primary between incumbent Rep. Celeste Maloy (currently representing the 2nd district) and former state Rep. Phil Lyman was held on June 23, 2026, with the winner heavily favored in the general election given the district's strong Republican lean (Cook Partisan Voting Index: R+21). Democratic nominee Kent Udell, a retired engineering professor, and third-party candidates Cassie Easley (Constitution), Michael Stoddard (Libertarian), and Ayden Scott (Unaffiliated) are also on the general election ballot.
polling_note: No public opinion polls were found for the general election as of mid-June 2026.

candidates.name: Celeste Maloy
candidates.summary: Celeste Maloy is a U.S. Representative first elected in a 2023 special election to represent Utah's 2nd Congressional District. Due to court-ordered redistricting, she is running in the newly drawn 3rd Congressional District and faced former state Rep. Phil Lyman in the June 23 Republican primary. Before Congress, she served as chief legal counsel to U.S. Rep. Chris Stewart and as a deputy county attorney for Washington County, and earlier worked as a soil conservationist for the Natural Resources Conservation Service.

candidates.name: Phil Lyman
candidates.summary: Phil Lyman is a former Utah State Representative (2019-2024) and a certified public accountant who ran for governor in 2024. He is known for his advocacy on public lands issues and was convicted for organizing an ATV protest ride in Recapture Canyon, for which he received a presidential pardon from Donald Trump in December 2020. Lyman faced incumbent Rep. Celeste Maloy in the June 23, 2026 Republican primary for Utah's newly drawn 3rd Congressional District.

candidates.name: Kent S. Udell
candidates.summary: Kent Udell is a mechanical engineer and professor emeritus who secured the Democratic nomination for Utah's 3rd Congressional District. He spent decades as a professor, researcher, and department chair at UC Berkeley and the University of Utah, where his research focused on groundwater remediation and sustainable energy systems. His campaign emphasizes water conservation, public lands stewardship, rule of law, and anti-corruption reforms.

candidates.name: Michael R. Stoddard
candidates.summary: Michael Stoddard is the Libertarian Party candidate for Utah's 3rd Congressional District in the 2026 general election. He filed as an election candidate with the Utah state election authority.

candidates.name: Cassie Easley
candidates.summary: Cassie Easley is the Constitution Party candidate for Utah's 3rd Congressional District in the 2026 general election. She previously ran as the Constitution Party candidate in Utah's 2nd Congressional District in 2024. Her campaign platform emphasizes constitutional governance and limited government.

candidates.name: Ayden Scott
candidates.summary: Ayden Scott is an unaffiliated candidate running for Utah's 3rd Congressional District in the 2026 general election. His campaign priorities include home ownership affordability, cost of living reduction, rural area support, and small business growth, with an emphasis on servant-leadership and community engagement through town halls across the district.

forecast.rationale: No public general-election polls are available, so this forecast relies on structural factors. The district's Cook Partisan Voting Index of R+21 indicates a heavily Republican-leaning seat in a strongly Republican state. The Republican primary (June 23, 2026) between incumbent Rep. Celeste Maloy and former state Rep. Phil Lyman has not yet concluded, but both candidates are credible Republicans and the winner will be heavily favored in the general election. Democratic nominee Kent Udell, a retired engineering professor, and third-party candidates (Constitution, Libertarian, Unaffiliated) lack the electoral infrastructure or partisan tailwinds to overcome such a strong GOP baseline. Confidence is medium rather than high due to the complete absence of polling and the pending primary outcome, but the district fundamentals overwhelmingly point to a safe Republican hold.
